docs.title: trueset
docs.text:
Catch the data problems every other check misses.

dbt tests, Great Expectations, and Soda all validate one table in isolation. They can't see the failures that matter most: a value that silently changed between two systems, or an extreme reading that's either a real event or an expensive error. trueset is built for exactly those — and every check is written once and runs on any engine — your warehouse as pushed-down SQL (Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, Postgres, Redshift), or locally on pandas and DuckDB.

pip install trueset

docs.title: The two things trueset does that single-table tools can't
docs.text:
• Cross-system reconciliation — validate one dataset against another system. Did the warehouse match the source after the load? The one capability GE / Soda / dbt tests aren't architected for. → Guide

  • Corroboration (newer) — when an extreme value is often the truth, not an error, judge it against supporting signals instead of a fixed threshold. → Guide

docs.title: Everything trueset ships
docs.text:
Area What you get Checks not_null, unique, in_set, in_range, matches_regex, row_count, no_duplicate_rows, columns_exist, metric Reconciliation row_count_parity, referential_integrity, value_parity — cross-system, cross-engine Ambiguity corroboration, source_corroboration, annotate, Adjudications, segment_bounds, robust MAD stats Backends one check on pandas, DuckDB, or any SQLAlchemy warehouse — verified identical, incl. real Postgres Pipelines validate at ingestion / in-flight / post-load; quarantine bad rows to a dead-letter sink Governance owner/sensitivity/regulation/tags; report --by; PII/PCI classification Monitoring freshness, volume/metric anomaly over run history, results persistence Authoring profile, suggest --calibrate, AI copilot (drafts checks; never judges data)

One trust rule throughout

AI can author and explain checks; only deterministic, auditable code ever decides pass/fail. Your validation stays reproducible and audit-ready.

Ready? → Getting started

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install trueset          # core (pandas)
pip install "trueset[sql]"   # + SQLAlchemy warehouses (Snowflake, BigQuery, Postgres…) + DuckDB

Requires Python 3.10+.

docs.title: Your first check suite
docs.text:
Checks are declared in YAML. Create checks.yml:

suite: orders_quality
checks:
  - type: not_null
    column: order_id
  - type: unique
    column: order_id
  - type: in_range
    column: amount
    min: 0
  - type: in_set
    column: status
    values: [pending, shipped, delivered, cancelled]
  - type: matches_regex
    column: email
    pattern: '[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+\.[^@\s]+'
    severity: warn        # warns, doesn't fail the run

Run it against a data file:

trueset run --data orders.csv --checks checks.yml

The command exits non-zero if any error-severity check fails, so it drops straight into CI, dbt, or Airflow. Add --json for machine-readable output.

docs.title: From Python
docs.text:
import pandas as pd
from trueset import validate_dataframe

df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv")
result = validate_dataframe(df, "checks.yml")

print(result.passed)        # False
print(result.to_dict())     # JSON-ready — ship to a warehouse or dashboard

Because a check only ever talks to the Backend protocol, the same checks.yml runs unchanged against a warehouse table:

trueset run --url "postgresql://user:pass@host/db" --table orders --checks checks.yml

docs.title: Severities
docs.text:
• error (default) — a failing check fails the run (non-zero exit). Gate CI with it.
  • warn — surfaces the problem but keeps the run green (exit 0).

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Cross-system reconciliation — the headline use case
  • Draft checks from your data with profile / suggest
  • Run in a pipeline and quarantine bad rows

docs.title: How trueset fits your stack
docs.text:
The one thing to understand about trueset: it travels with your data. The same check runs in your pipeline before data lands, inside your warehouse after it lands, and across two systems to prove they agree.

That's the difference from a warehouse-only tool like dbt, which can only test data that is already in the warehouse.

  SOURCE              INGESTION / PIPELINE            WAREHOUSE
  (DB, API,    ──►    Python / CSV / stream    ──►    Snowflake · BigQuery ·
   files)             (Airflow, Spark, CI)            Postgres · Databricks · …
                             │                               │
                     ✅ trueset here                  ✅ trueset here
                     catch bad data                   push checks down as SQL,
                     BEFORE it lands                  data never leaves
                             │                               │
                             └──── ✅ trueset reconciles the two ────┘
                              did the warehouse match the source?

docs.title: In your pipeline (shift-left)
docs.text:
trueset is a pip install, so it runs as an ordinary step in your pipeline — in Airflow, Spark, dbt's surrounding orchestration, or a CI job — on a DataFrame, a file, or a stream. Because it runs before the load, it can stop bad data from ever reaching the warehouse, and its exit code gates the step:

trueset run --data orders.csv --checks checks.yml   # non-zero exit on failure

from trueset import validate_dataframe
result = validate_dataframe(df, "checks.yml")        # inside a pipeline task
if not result.passed:
    ...                                              # route / block / alert

docs.title: In your warehouse (in place, as SQL)
docs.text:
Point the same checks.yml at a live table and trueset pushes each check down as SQL — so the full table never leaves the warehouse. Only the source changes from --data to --url + --table:

trueset run --url "snowflake://…" --table orders --checks checks.yml

This is the layer dbt also operates in. trueset works with any SQLAlchemy-supported database — Snowflake, BigQuery, Postgres, Databricks, Redshift, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle, ClickHouse, … — the command is identical; only the URL and the installed driver change.

docs.title: Across systems (reconciliation)
docs.text:
The part most tools can't do: check that one system matches another — did the warehouse actually equal the source after the load? Row counts can match while values silently drift; value_parity catches it.

trueset reconcile --data warehouse_orders.csv --checks reconcile.yml \
  --ref source=source_orders.csv

docs.title: trueset vs. dbt, at a glance
docs.text:
In your pipeline (pre-load) In your warehouse (post-load) Across two systems dbt tests ❌ needs data already loaded ✅ ❌ trueset ✅ ✅ ✅

They're complementary: keep your dbt tests (trueset can even import them), and use trueset to extend the same quality bar earlier in the pipeline and across systems.

In one line: dbt tests live where your data already is; trueset travels with your data — before the load, after the load, and between systems.

docs.title: Test drive — an end-to-end case study
docs.text:
Run trueset the way a real user would, start to finish, in ~15 minutes. The story: you're a data engineer on an e-commerce team. Orders flow from a production Postgres database into a warehouse, and you need to trust them.

Everything here uses the sample files in examples/, so clone the repo (or download that folder) first:

git clone https://github.com/trueset-dev/trueset.git
cd trueset
pip install "trueset[sql]"

docs.title: 1. Your first check (a file)
docs.text:
Validate a CSV against a handful of rules:

trueset run --data examples/orders.csv --checks examples/checks.yml

You'll see a table — some checks pass, some fail — and the process exits non-zero when an error-severity check fails. That exit code is what gates a CI job, an Airflow task, or a pre-load step. Good data passes; bad data stops.

Don't want to write checks by hand? trueset suggest --data examples/orders.csv drafts a starter suite from your data for you to review.

docs.title: 2. Cross-system reconciliation (the headline)
docs.text:
The thing single-table tools can't do: check that a dataset matches another system — did the warehouse match the source after the load?

trueset reconcile \
  --data   examples/warehouse_orders.csv \
  --checks examples/reconcile.yml \
  --ref    source=examples/source_orders.csv

value_parity reports all three failure modes at once: values that differ on shared keys, keys only in the warehouse, and keys only in the source. Row counts can match while values silently drift — this is what catches it.

docs.title: 3. Run it against a real warehouse (Postgres)
docs.text:
The same checks run in-place on any SQL warehouse via SQLAlchemy — Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, Redshift, Postgres — pushed down as SQL, so data never moves. Let's prove it on Postgres. (Have Docker? Spin one up; otherwise point the URL at any Postgres you have.)

# a throwaway Postgres on port 5433
docker run -d --name trueset-pg -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=postgres -p 5433:5432 postgres:16

# load the sample orders into it
python - <<'PY'
import pandas as pd
from sqlalchemy import create_engine
e = create_engine("postgresql+psycopg://postgres:postgres@localhost:5433/postgres")
pd.read_csv("examples/orders.csv").to_sql("orders", e, index=False, if_exists="replace")
print("loaded orders into Postgres")
PY

# validate the live table — identical checks, now pushed down as SQL
trueset run \
  --url   "postgresql+psycopg://postgres:postgres@localhost:5433/postgres" \
  --table orders \
  --checks examples/checks.yml

Same suite, same verdict — in memory or in the warehouse. (Swap the URL for snowflake://…, bigquery://…, databricks://…, etc. with the matching SQLAlchemy driver installed.)

docs.title: 4. Already have dbt tests? Adopt them, don't rewrite them
docs.text:
Point trueset at a dbt schema.yml and it converts your existing tests into a runnable trueset suite — not_null/unique map directly, accepted_values → in_set, relationships → referential_integrity.

# a minimal dbt schema.yml
cat > schema.yml <<'YAML'
version: 2
models:
  - name: orders
    columns:
      - name: order_id
        tests:
          - not_null
          - unique
      - name: status
        tests:
          - accepted_values:
              values: [pending, shipped, delivered, cancelled]
YAML

# convert dbt tests -> a trueset suite
trueset import-dbt --schema schema.yml --model orders --out from_dbt.yml

# run the converted suite (anywhere — file, or the Postgres table from step 3)
trueset run --data examples/orders.csv --checks from_dbt.yml

Now the same checks run in CI, in your pipeline, and cross-warehouse — without leaving dbt behind.

docs.title: 5. Quarantine the bad rows (shift-left)
docs.text:
trueset doesn't just flag bad data — it hands you the bad rows so your pipeline can dead-letter them and keep the clean ones moving:

trueset run \
  --data examples/orders.csv \
  --checks examples/checks.yml \
  --quarantine bad_rows.csv \
  --save sqlite:///trueset_history.db

bad_rows.csv now holds the failing rows (with a _trueset_reasons column), ready for a dead-letter sink — and the run, including how many rows were rerouted, is saved to the history store.

docs.title: 6. See it all — the dashboard
docs.text:
Run a few suites with --save pointing at the same store, then open the centralized Data Trust view:

trueset dashboard --open

One trust score, the shift-left data flow (rows checked vs. rerouted), health by quality dimension, your datasets, and an incident feed — including volume anomalies the engine catches that no rule would (data that passes every check but whose row count quietly collapsed). See Dashboard.

docs.title: Clean up
docs.text:
docker rm -f trueset-pg        # if you started the throwaway Postgres
rm -f from_dbt.yml bad_rows.csv trueset_history.db trueset-dashboard.html schema.yml

That's the full loop: validate → reconcile → warehouse → dbt → quarantine → dashboard. Found a rough edge? Open an issue — that feedback is exactly what shapes the roadmap.

docs.title: Trusting volatile data
docs.text:
When an extreme value might be the truth, not an error.

Most data-quality tools are built on a quiet assumption: an outlier is a mistake. Set a threshold, reject anything past it. That works for a country_code or an email — and fails badly for data where a spike is often real:

A natural-gas price triples during a cold snap. A sensor reading jumps when the machine actually gets hot. Checkout traffic 10×s on launch day. Blood pressure spikes because the patient is genuinely in distress.

A fixed threshold flags the real event as an error (false positive — you cry wolf and get ignored) or it's loose enough to miss a genuine bad value (a silent error slips through). In volatile domains you can't win with rules alone. You have to answer a harder question: is this extreme corroborated?

That's what this part of trueset is for. It doesn't pretend to "know" whether an extreme is real — it surfaces and quantifies the ambiguity so a human or a downstream system can decide, and it stops re-asking once someone has.

docs.title: Where this shows up
docs.text:
The pattern — legitimate extremes mixed with real errors — is not a commodities thing. It's everywhere volatile:

Domain A real extreme looks like… The silent error looks like… Commodities / markets cold-snap price spike, backed by demand/volume a one-feed phantom tick no other source confirms IoT / sensors temperature spike when load genuinely rises a stuck/garbled reading with no matching signal Energy / utilities demand surge in a heatwave a meter misread Observability / web traffic launch-day or incident spike a logging double-count Healthcare / vitals a genuine clinical event a probe artifact Fraud / risk a real large transaction a decimal-point data-entry error Ad / marketing a viral-moment conversion jump duplicate event tracking

If your data has this shape, the four moves below apply unchanged — only the "corroborating signal" differs (volume, a sibling sensor, a second feed, …).

docs.title: 1. Corroboration — tell a real extreme from a bad value
docs.text:
Judge a suspicious value against a supporting signal, not in isolation. A real price spike shows up in volume too; a stuck sensor's jump doesn't match the load.

- type: corroboration
  column: price
  corroborate_with: [demand]   # trust the spike only if demand backs it
  severity: warn               # surface it — real extremes happen; don't block

day 18: price=9.8, demand=140  ->  trusted (corroborated — demand backs it)
day 19: price=9.9, demand=51   ->  FLAGGED (uncorroborated — a lone bad tick)

The real event passes; only the unsupported extreme is flagged. (Cross-feed variant: source_corroboration confirms against an independent source instead of a sibling column — a move shows up in both feeds; a phantom shows up in one.)

docs.title: 2. Annotate-and-flow — score, don't block
docs.text:
Volatile data usually can't be blocked — a trading desk, an ops dashboard, a monitoring system needs the full picture. So instead of dropping rows, attach a quality score and let everything flow:

from trueset import annotate
scored = annotate(df, "checks.yml", key="day")
# every row gets _trueset_quality (0..1) and _trueset_flags; nothing is dropped

Downstream decides what to do with low-quality rows (weight them down, review them, alert) — the data keeps moving.

docs.title: 3. Adjudication — review once, stop re-flagging
docs.text:
The thing that kills trust in a DQ tool is re-flagging the same known-good event every single run. When a human rules an extreme valid, record it:

from trueset import Adjudications
adj = Adjudications()
adj.mark_valid("in_range(price)", 18, note="real cold-snap demand spike")
adj.save("adjudications.json")          # auditable, git-committable
annotate(df, "checks.yml", key="day", adjudications=adj)   # suppressed from now on

docs.title: 4. Context-aware ranges — not one global threshold
docs.text:
A legitimate regime in one segment shouldn't be judged by another's baseline. Derive the expected band per segment (region, regime, season, device):

from trueset import segment_bounds
segment_bounds(df, "price", "region")
# OK: [2.68, 3.72]   TX: [2.58, 3.62]   ← each segment judged on its own history

All four rest on robust statistics (trueset.robust_z / MAD, with a flat-baseline fallback) — a defensible basis, never a hand-picked number.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
A runnable, end-to-end version of all four moves (the natural-gas example above) ships in the repo:

python examples/ambiguity_demo.py

For the full YAML/API reference, see Corroboration & ambiguity.

Honest status

The corroboration / source_corroboration checks materialize the analyzed columns; annotate and segment_bounds operate on an in-memory (pandas) DataFrame today. That's fine for market/sensor data volumes; pushing the statistics down into the warehouse for very large tables is on the roadmap.

docs.title: Corroboration & ambiguity
docs.text:
Newer / experimental

These features are the newest part of trueset. The checks run on any backend (they materialize the analyzed columns); annotate and segment_bounds operate on an in-memory DataFrame. See the roadmap.

Some data — commodities, markets, sensors — has a hard property: an extreme value is often the truth, not an error (a cold-snap demand spike, a geopolitical event, a market move). A fixed threshold can't tell a real extreme from a mistake. trueset's job here is to surface and quantify the ambiguity, not pretend to resolve it.

New here? Start with the showcase — Trusting volatile data — for the pattern and where it applies (markets, IoT, energy, observability, healthcare, fraud…). This page is the YAML/API reference.

docs.title: Corroboration — is a suspicious value supported?
docs.text:
Judge an outlier against supporting signals, not in isolation. A real price spike shows up in volume too; a silent bad tick doesn't.

- type: corroboration
  column: price
  corroborate_with: [volume]   # trust the spike only if volume backs it
  z: 3.5                       # robust-outlier threshold on the primary
  min_support: 1               # how many corroborators must agree
  severity: warn               # surface it — real extremes happen, don't block

docs.title: Cross-source corroboration — do 2+ sources agree?
docs.text:
Corroborate against an independent feed instead of a sibling column:

- type: source_corroboration
  column: price
  key: date
  reference: source_b          # resolved at run time like a reconciliation ref
  rel_tol: 0.1                 # confirmed if the other source agrees within 10%
  severity: warn

A real move shows up in both feeds; a one-source phantom is surfaced.

docs.title: Annotate-and-flow — score, don't block
docs.text:
Market data often can't be blocked — you need a full view. Instead of dropping bad rows, attach a quality score and let everything flow:

from trueset import annotate
scored = annotate(df, "checks.yml", key="day")
# adds _trueset_quality (0..1) and _trueset_flags (checks each row failed)

or from the CLI:

trueset annotate --data ticks.csv --checks checks.yml --out scored.csv

Nothing is dropped; downstream decides what to do with low-quality rows.

docs.title: Adjudications — review once, stop re-flagging
docs.text:
When a human rules a flag "actually valid," record it so future runs don't re-flag it — the feedback loop that kills repeat false positives:

from trueset import Adjudications
adj = Adjudications()
adj.mark_valid("in_range(price)", "2026-03-09", note="real cold-snap spike")
adj.save("adjudications.json")            # auditable, git-committable

annotate(df, "checks.yml", key="day", adjudications=adj)   # suppressed going forward

docs.title: Context-aware ranges
docs.text:
A legitimate seasonal spike in one segment shouldn't trip a global threshold set by the others. Derive an expected band per segment:

from trueset import segment_bounds
segment_bounds(df, "price", "region")
# {'north': {'min': .., 'max': .., 'n': ..}, 'south': {...}}

All of it rests on robust statistics (trueset.robust_z / MAD, with a flat-baseline fallback) — a defensible basis, never a hand-picked number.

Runnable end-to-end example: examples/ambiguity_demo.py.

docs.title: Authoring checks
docs.text: You don't have to write every check by hand. trueset can draft a suite from your data — deterministically, or with an AI copilot — and every proposed check is validated through the same registry, so the output is always something you can read, trust, and commit.

docs.title: Profile your data
docs.text:
trueset profile --data orders.csv

Shows per-column stats and an inferred semantic type (email / uuid / url / datetime / categorical / numeric / …) plus a suggested sensitivity.

docs.title: Draft a suite (deterministic, no AI)
docs.text:
trueset suggest --data orders.csv                 # rule-based draft, always safe
trueset suggest --data orders.csv --out checks.yml

docs.title: Auto-calibrated thresholds
docs.text:
Rather than hand-picking limits, derive them from the data — numeric in_range bounds (from the 1st/99th percentiles, widened so current data passes) and a row-count volume band, emitted as warn for you to review:

trueset suggest --data orders.csv --calibrate

Run calibration on known-good data

Calibration learns from the sample — representative input in means sensible thresholds out.

docs.title: AI copilot
docs.text:
The copilot turns a data profile or a plain-English intent into checks:

export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=…
trueset suggest --data orders.csv --ai --out checks.yml
trueset suggest --data orders.csv --describe "amount can't be negative; \
    status is one of pending/shipped/delivered/cancelled"

The trust rule that makes AI safe here

The copilot only ever authors checks. Every spec it returns is passed through the deterministic registry (build_check) — anything it hallucinates or misconfigures is discarded before it can reach your data. The AI is never in the runtime pass/fail path, so your validation stays deterministic and auditable. The model is injected as a plain callable, so it's provider-agnostic and fully testable without a key.

docs.title: Backends & warehouses
docs.text: The core bet: write a check once, run it on any engine. A check never touches pandas, DuckDB, or SQL directly — it only calls a small Backend protocol. To support a new engine you implement one class; not a single check is rewritten.

docs.title: Available backends
docs.text:
Backend Use it for Extra PandasBackend in-memory DataFrames (pipelines, tests) — DuckDBBackend local/embedded SQL, Parquet [sql] SQLAlchemyBackend Postgres, MySQL/MariaDB, SQLite, Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, … [sql]

On the SQL backends, single-table checks are pushed down as SELECT count(*) … WHERE … executed inside the database — those tables never move across the wire.

Two honest limits

  • Cross-system reconciliation: when both sides share one database, value_parity and referential_integrity push down as SQL (inner join + anti-joins) — nothing is materialized. Across different engines (what makes CSV-vs-warehouse checks possible), they compare the key + compared columns in memory; cross-engine hashing to avoid that is on the roadmap.
  • Regex pushdown (matches_regex) is wired for Postgres, Redshift, MySQL/MariaDB and SQLite. Other dialects (e.g. Snowflake, BigQuery) raise a clear "not yet wired" error for that one check type; everything else runs.

docs.title: Run against your warehouse
docs.text:
trueset run --url "postgresql://user:pass@host:5432/db" --table orders --checks checks.yml

From Python:

from sqlalchemy import create_engine
from trueset import Suite
from trueset.backends.sqlalchemy_backend import SQLAlchemyBackend

engine = create_engine("postgresql+psycopg://…")
result = Suite.from_yaml("checks.yml").run(SQLAlchemyBackend(engine, "orders"))

docs.title: Portability, proven
docs.text:
The whole thesis is tested, not asserted. The identical suite, run on pandas (in-memory) and on DuckDB (SQL pushed into the database), returns the same verdict — and the cross-engine parity is enforced in CI, including against a real Postgres 16 (exercising the dialect-specific paths: the ~ regex operator, casts, window functions).

check                   pandas      duckdb      match
------------------------------------------------------
row_count_parity        pass(0)     pass(0)     OK
referential_integrity   fail(1)     fail(1)     OK
value_parity            fail(3)     fail(3)     OK

docs.title: Adding a backend
docs.text: Implement every method in backends/base.py (mirror duckdb_backend.py), then add a cross-engine parity test asserting it agrees with pandas on the example suites. That's the entire contribution — no check changes. See CONTRIBUTING.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text: Single-source checks validate one dataset. Each is declared in YAML with a type and its parameters, plus an optional severity (error default, or warn).

docs.title: Built-in checks
docs.text: Type Parameters Fails when columns_exist columns: [str] a listed column is missing not_null column the column has null values unique column the column has duplicate values in_set column, values: [...] a value isn't in the allowed set in_range column, min?, max? a numeric value is out of range matches_regex column, pattern a value doesn't fully match the pattern row_count min?, max? the row count is outside the range no_duplicate_rows subset?: [str] duplicate rows exist (optionally on a subset) metric column, agg, equals?/tolerance?, min?, max? an aggregate is off target

docs.title: The metric check
docs.text:
Validate an aggregate — for metrics/report validation ("total revenue ≈ X", "avg order value in [10, 100]"):

- type: metric
  column: amount
  agg: sum            # sum | avg | min | max | count
  equals: 15000
  tolerance: 0.01     # within 1%
- type: metric
  column: amount
  agg: avg
  min: 10
  max: 100

It runs as a pushed-down aggregate, so it works identically on pandas, DuckDB, and any SQL warehouse.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Every check produces a structured, JSON-serializable CheckResult (check, status, severity, column, observed, failing_rows, total_rows, message). A SuiteResult bundles them with a passed verdict and counts — ready for CI, a dashboard, or a warehouse table.

result = validate_dataframe(df, "checks.yml")
result.passed          # bool — False if any error-severity check failed
result.counts          # {"pass": .., "fail": .., "error": .., "warn": ..}
result.to_dict()       # full JSON evidence

See the check reference for every field, and Authoring to draft a suite from your data automatically.

docs.title: Dashboard — the centralized Data Trust view
docs.text:
trueset dashboard turns your run history into one self-contained HTML page: a single Data Trust Score, the shift-left data flow (rows checked vs. rerouted to quarantine), health by quality dimension (freshness, completeness, validity, uniqueness, volume, reconciliation), a dense asset table, and an incident feed — including anomalies the engine catches that no single-table check would (a dataset that passes every rule but whose volume quietly collapsed).

It reads data trueset already produces — no server, no cloud, no extra dependencies. It's the open-source seed of the hosted hub.

docs.title: Use it
docs.text:
Save your runs to a history store, then open the dashboard:

# 1. save each run to a store (SQLite locally, or Postgres/Snowflake for a team)
trueset run --data orders.csv --checks checks.yml --save sqlite:///trueset_history.db

# 2. open the centralized view
trueset dashboard --open

Options:

Flag Default What it does --store sqlite:///trueset_history.db Results store to read (any SQLAlchemy URL). --out trueset-dashboard.html Where to write the HTML. --open off Open it in your browser when done. --limit 400 Max recent runs to read.

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text:
• Data Trust Score + a trust-over-time chart, with the change over the window.
  • Data flow — rows checked vs. rerouted to a dead-letter sink. Populate the rerouted number by running with --quarantine (see Pipelines & quarantine).
  • Quality by dimension — each check type maps to a dimension; freshness is framed as an SLA.
  • Volume-anomaly detection — surfaces the engine's anomaly detection over run history (a silent failure: data that passes every check but whose row volume deviates from its baseline).
  • Monitored datasets — status, trust, freshness, rows, rerouted, checks, trend.
  • Open incidents — failing checks, freshness breaches, and volume anomalies, most-severe first.

docs.title: Populate it realistically
docs.text: The dashboard gets richer as history accumulates. Run your suites on a schedule (cron, Airflow, a CI job) with --save pointing at the same store, and --quarantine where you dead-letter bad rows, so the flow and trend panels fill in. For a team, point --store at a shared Postgres instead of a local SQLite file and everyone reads the same view.

docs.title: Governance & classification
docs.text: trueset is not a catalog or a lineage graph (that's DataHub / OpenMetadata / Collibra territory — compose with them, don't rebuild them). It owns the half those tools are weak on: enforcement and evidence. Governance here is optional metadata on checks, not a new subsystem.

docs.title: Metadata on a check
docs.text:
Any check may carry optional governance fields — they're additive and change nothing about how the check runs:

- type: not_null
  column: customer_ssn
  severity: error
  owner: risk-team                 # accountable party
  sensitivity: pii                 # public|internal|confidential|pii|pci|phi
  regulation: [gdpr, ccpa]         # free list of regime tags
  tags: [customer, identity]
  description: "SSN required for KYC"

The metadata rides onto every CheckResult and serializes into the JSON evidence, so a persisted run becomes an auditable record: dataset X met policy Y on date Z.

docs.title: Policy reports
docs.text:
Once results carry metadata, governance reporting is just grouping:

trueset report --data orders.csv --checks governed_checks.yml --by sensitivity
trueset report --data orders.csv --checks governed_checks.yml --by owner
trueset report --data orders.csv --checks governed_checks.yml --by regulation

This surfaces, e.g., all failing checks on PII columns owned by the risk team — directly from the results you already produce.

docs.title: Data classification
docs.text:
trueset profile infers a suggested sensitivity for high-precision patterns — email, phone, US SSN, credit card (Luhn, even as a bare integer), IBAN → pii / pci:

trueset profile --data customers.csv     # shows an inferred sensitivity column

trueset suggest then pre-tags the drafted checks with the suggested sensitivity.

Suggested, never imposed

Both the deterministic profiler and the AI copilot only suggest tags. trueset never auto-applies a classification — a human reviews and commits it, the same trust rule as checks.

docs.title: Monitoring & history
docs.text: Turn one-shot validation into continuous monitoring: persist every run, then watch for staleness and drift over time.

docs.title: Freshness
docs.text:
An ordinary check — the newest timestamp must be recent (catches stale pipelines):

- type: freshness
  column: created_at
  max_age_hours: 6        # fail if the table hasn't updated in 6 hours

Runs on every backend via a pushed-down max().

docs.title: Results history
docs.text:
Persist runs to any SQLAlchemy database as an auditable trail:

trueset run --data orders.csv --checks checks.yml --save "postgresql://…/trueset_history"
trueset history --store "postgresql://…/trueset_history"

Two tables (trueset_runs, trueset_results) keep verdicts, counts, row volume, and full per-check evidence.

docs.title: Anomaly detection
docs.text:
trueset monitor trends a metric against the baseline of past runs and exits non-zero on an anomaly — a silent 90% drop in rows is caught even when every row that is there passes every check:

trueset monitor --store "$H" --suite orders --metric rows --method mad
trueset monitor --store "$H" --suite orders --metric failing_rows --check not_null --column email
  • --metric — rows, failing_rows, or total_rows (with --check / --column to pick a specific check's trend).
  • --method — zscore (mean/std) or mad (median-absolute-deviation, robust when a few past runs were themselves outliers).

Detection is deterministic and explainable — never a black box.

docs.title: Orchestration — run trueset in your pipeline
docs.text:
trueset is a pip install and a CLI with a meaningful exit code, so it drops into any orchestrator as an ordinary step. There's nothing trueset-specific to learn on the orchestrator side: run a check, and let a non-zero exit (any error-severity failure) fail the task and stop bad data moving downstream.

Two patterns cover almost everything:

  • Gate — run a check as its own task; if it fails, the pipeline stops.
  • Quarantine-and-continue — split the batch, load the clean rows, send the bad ones to a dead-letter sink, keep going.

Runnable references live in the repo: examples/airflow_dq_dag.py and examples/dagster_dq_check.py.

docs.title: Simplest — a gate with BashOperator
docs.text:
from airflow.operators.bash import BashOperator

check = BashOperator(
    task_id="dq_gate",
    # non-zero exit on any error-severity failure fails the task
    bash_command="trueset run --data /data/orders.csv --checks /dq/checks.yml "
                 "--save postgresql+psycopg://warehouse/dq",
)
extract >> check >> load          # load only runs if the gate passes

docs.title: In-memory — PythonOperator with the API
docs.text:
from airflow.exceptions import AirflowFailException
from trueset import validate_dataframe

def dq_gate(**ctx):
    df = ctx["ti"].xcom_pull(task_ids="extract")      # a DataFrame
    result = validate_dataframe(df, "/dq/checks.yml")
    if not result.passed:
        raise AirflowFailException(f"data quality failed: {result.to_dict()}")

docs.title: Quarantine-and-continue
docs.text:
from trueset import Suite, split

def load_clean(**ctx):
    df = ctx["ti"].xcom_pull(task_ids="extract")
    sp = split(df, Suite.from_yaml("/dq/checks.yml"))
    sp.bad_annotated().to_csv("/dead_letter/bad.csv", index=False)   # reasons attached
    sp.good.to_sql("orders", warehouse_engine, if_exists="append")  # clean rows flow

docs.title: Dagster
docs.text:
Model data quality as a first-class asset check so it shows up on the asset:

from dagster import asset_check, AssetCheckResult
from trueset import validate_dataframe

@asset_check(asset="orders")
def orders_quality(orders):                 # `orders` is the upstream asset's value
    result = validate_dataframe(orders, "checks.yml")
    return AssetCheckResult(
        passed=result.passed,
        metadata=result.to_dict(),          # evidence surfaces in the Dagster UI
    )

A failing check blocks downstream assets (or warns), per the check's severity.

docs.title: Prefect
docs.text:
from prefect import task
from trueset import validate_dataframe

@task
def dq_gate(df):
    result = validate_dataframe(df, "checks.yml")
    if not result.passed:
        raise ValueError(f"data quality failed: {result.to_dict()}")
    return df

docs.title: CI (GitHub Actions)
docs.text:
trueset ships a composite Action, so a pull request can be gated on data quality:

- uses: trueset-dev/trueset@main
  with:
    data: data/orders.csv
    checks: dq/checks.yml

Or without the Action — just the CLI, which works in any CI system:

- run: pip install "trueset[sql]"
- run: trueset run --data data/orders.csv --checks dq/checks.yml

docs.title: In the warehouse
docs.text:
Every recipe above works against a live warehouse table too — swap --data for --url + --table (CLI), so the checks run as SQL where the data already lives:

trueset run --url "$WAREHOUSE_URL" --table orders --checks dq/checks.yml

See How it fits your stack for pipeline-vs-warehouse, and Pipelines & quarantine for the routing details.

docs.title: Pipelines & quarantine
docs.text:
trueset is a library first, not a warehouse-only CLI. Because the pandas backend accepts any DataFrame, you can validate data at every stage of a pipeline — not just after loading.

Where Works? How At ingestion / pre-load ✅ validate the DataFrame before it lands Mid-transform (Airflow/Dagster/Prefect task, Lambda, script) ✅ validate_dataframe(df, suite) on any intermediate frame Post-load / in the warehouse ✅ SQLAlchemyBackend — pushed-down SQL Across the boundary (source vs warehouse) ✅ reconciliation Per-event streaming ⚠️ batch / micro-batch oriented; validate each batch Native Spark (in-cluster) ❌ roadmap — today .toPandas() or push to the warehouse

docs.title: Shift-left: a quality gate at ingestion
docs.text:
Stop bad data before it ever reaches storage:

from trueset import validate_dataframe

df = extract_from_api()                        # your ingestion step
result = validate_dataframe(df, "checks.yml")  # same suite, in-memory
if not result.passed:
    raise ValueError(f"bad batch, not loading: {result.counts}")
load_to_warehouse(df)                          # only reached if data is clean

docs.title: Quarantine / dead-letter routing
docs.text:
trueset detects; it never silently reroutes your data. split() gives you the material to route with — the failing rows partitioned from the clean ones:

from trueset import split

result = split(df, "checks.yml")
load_to_warehouse(result.good)          # clean rows through
dead_letter(result.bad_annotated())     # bad rows + a _trueset_reasons column

By default only error-severity checks divert a row (include_warnings=True to opt in). From the CLI, write failing rows to a file:

trueset run --data batch.csv --checks checks.yml --quarantine bad.csv

For the annotate-and-flow alternative (score every row, block nothing), see Corroboration & ambiguity.

docs.title: Cross-system reconciliation
docs.text:
The capability no single-table tool (dbt tests, Great Expectations, Soda, Pandera) is architected to express, and whose only open-source option (data-diff) was archived in 2024: validate one dataset against another system.

This is the failure that passes every row-level check: the warehouse table looks internally valid, but it silently dropped rows, gained phantom rows, or corrupted a value somewhere between the source and the load. Reconciliation catches it.

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
A reconciliation check holds a second (reference) backend and compares. Because checks only talk to the Backend protocol, the two sides can be different engines — a CSV export vs. a Postgres table, a source database vs. your warehouse.

trueset reconcile \
  --data   warehouse_orders.csv \
  --checks reconcile.yml \
  --ref    source=source_orders.csv

suite: warehouse_vs_source
checks:
  - type: row_count_parity        # counts agree within tolerance
    reference: source
    tolerance: 0.0

  - type: referential_integrity   # every key traces back to the source
    column: order_id
    reference: source
    ref_column: id

  - type: value_parity            # join on key, compare actual values
    key: order_id
    columns: [amount, status]
    reference: source
    ref_key: id

docs.title: The three checks
docs.text:
Check Catches row_count_parity the load dropped or duplicated rows (counts diverge beyond tolerance) referential_integrity orphan keys — rows whose key never existed in the source value_parity value drift on shared keys, keys only in one side, and duplicate keys

value_parity reports every failure mode in one result:

{
  "mismatched_values": 1,
  "only_in_primary": 1,
  "only_in_reference": 1,
  "duplicate_keys_primary": 0,
  "duplicate_keys_reference": 0,
  "compared_keys": 3
}

Passing row_count_parity alone proves nothing about contents

Two datasets can have identical counts and completely different rows. That's exactly why value_parity and referential_integrity exist alongside it.

docs.title: Comparing across engines: type drift and tolerance
docs.text:
Values are compared type-aware, so cross-engine storage differences don't read as false mismatches: Decimal('10.00') (a warehouse NUMERIC), 10.0 (a CSV float) and '10.0' (text) are equal, and two missing values (NULL/NaN) are equal while one-missing differs. For rounding, add an absolute tolerance:

  - type: value_parity
    key: order_id
    columns: [amount]
    reference: source
    tolerance: 0.01          # amounts within 1 cent are considered equal

What counts as the same value

Numeric comparison (Decimal vs float vs numeric text, plus tolerance) applies when at least one side is a real number — a warehouse NUMERIC 19.99 and a CSV float 19.99 match exactly. Two values that are both non-numeric text are compared literally, so a leading-zero SKU '007' never equals '7'. Mixed non-numeric types — e.g. a date compared against a differently-formatted date string — are compared as text; if your two systems format such a column differently, cast it on one side (or compare a normalized column) rather than relying on automatic coercion.

docs.title: Reconcile two SQL systems directly
docs.text:
Both the primary and the references can be live SQL tables — reconcile a warehouse against its source database without exporting anything:

trueset reconcile \
  --url  "postgresql://…/warehouse" --table orders \
  --checks reconcile.yml \
  --ref  "source=postgresql://…/source::orders"

docs.title: Data contracts
docs.text: A reconciliation suite is a cross-system contract between a producer and a consumer. Give it a name, an owner, and put it in CI, and you have contract enforcement — the hardest part (the comparison) already exists.

docs.title: Check reference
docs.text: Every check accepts an optional severity (error default, or warn) and the optional governance fields (owner, sensitivity, regulation, tags, description).

docs.title: Single-source checks
docs.text: Type Parameters columns_exist columns: [str] not_null column: str unique column: str in_set column: str, values: [any] in_range column: str, min?: number, max?: number matches_regex column: str, pattern: str row_count min?: int, max?: int no_duplicate_rows subset?: [str] metric column: str, agg: sum\|avg\|min\|max\|count, equals?, tolerance?, min?, max? freshness column: str, max_age_hours: number

docs.title: Reconciliation checks
docs.text:
Each takes a reference: naming another dataset, resolved at run time.

Type Parameters row_count_parity reference: str, tolerance?: float referential_integrity column, reference, ref_column value_parity key, columns: [str], reference, ref_key?, ref_columns?

docs.title: Ambiguity checks
docs.text:
(newer / experimental — see the guide)

Type Parameters corroboration column, corroborate_with: [str], z?, support_z?, min_support?, directional? source_corroboration column, key, reference, ref_column?, ref_key?, z?, rel_tol?

docs.title: CheckResult fields
docs.text:
Field Meaning check the check type status pass | fail | error (the check itself couldn't run) severity error | warn column the column checked (if any) observed what was measured (count, or a structured detail) failing_rows / total_rows counts message human-readable summary meta governance metadata (when set)

A SuiteResult bundles results with .passed, .counts, and .to_dict().

docs.title: CLI reference
docs.text:
All commands exit non-zero when an error-severity check fails (except annotate, which never blocks). Add --json to run / reconcile for machine-readable output.

trueset --help
trueset list-checks         # every available check type

docs.title: run
docs.text:
Validate a dataset (a file, or a live SQL table) against a suite.

trueset run --data orders.csv --checks checks.yml
trueset run --url "postgresql://…/db" --table orders --checks checks.yml
trueset run --data batch.csv --checks checks.yml --quarantine bad.csv   # write failing rows

docs.title: reconcile
docs.text:
Validate a dataset against other systems. See Reconciliation.

trueset reconcile --data warehouse.csv --checks reconcile.yml --ref source=source.csv
trueset reconcile --url "…/warehouse" --table orders --checks reconcile.yml \
  --ref "source=…/source::orders"

docs.title: annotate
docs.text:
Score every row and keep them all (annotate-and-flow).

trueset annotate --data ticks.csv --checks checks.yml --out scored.csv
trueset annotate --data ticks.csv --checks checks.yml --key day --adjudications adj.json

docs.title: report
docs.text:
Group pass/fail by a governance dimension.

trueset report --data orders.csv --checks governed.yml --by sensitivity   # or owner | regulation

docs.title: profile / suggest
docs.text:
Draft checks from your data. See Authoring.

trueset profile --data orders.csv
trueset suggest --data orders.csv --calibrate --out checks.yml
trueset suggest --data orders.csv --describe "amount can't be negative"     # needs ANTHROPIC_API_KEY

docs.title: monitor / history
docs.text:
Persist runs and detect anomalies over time. See Monitoring.

trueset run … --save "postgresql://…/trueset_history"
trueset history --store "postgresql://…/trueset_history"
trueset monitor --store "$H" --suite orders --metric rows --method mad

docs.title: import-dbt
docs.text:
Convert dbt column tests into a trueset suite.

trueset import-dbt --schema schema.yml --model orders --out checks.yml

not_null/unique map directly, accepted_values → in_set, relationships → referential_integrity; severity is preserved; unmappable tests are reported, not silently dropped.
